stories.headline: Saudi authorities say attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300
stories.title: Saudi authorities say attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300
stories.summary: Cairo, Oct 11: Saudi authorities say an attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more. According to a statement by Saudi authorities, the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, and one each from Palestine, the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan. It said some of those injured were in critical condition. The international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, was attacked again Saturday as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen. The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. On Saturday, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights and many people were wounded, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media. “We may. We're going to look at it,” Trump said of intervening. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly.” The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital. Riyadh airport operations have been suspended Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended and the extent of injuries and damage was being assessed. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed. Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport. The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday. Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships. Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that. Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran. Officials have said US assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis. On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region. Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.” Flight disruptions are growing The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations. At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.” The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.

stories.headline: Chief Justice calls for greater representation of women in legal profession
stories.title: Chief Justice calls for greater representation of women in legal profession
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, on Saturday called for greater participation of women in the legal profession and urged judicial institutions to embrace technology to meet changing societal expectations. Addressing a felicitation programme organised by the Kashmir Advocates Association at the District Court Complex in Srinagar, the Chief Justice said encouraging women advocates and ensuring their active participation in the legal fraternity was essential for its progress. His remarks came as the Association announced that it had agreed in principle to induct five women lawyers into its Executive Committee, with the decision to be formalised shortly. Welcoming the move, Justice Bhati recalled the pioneering contribution of Cornelia Sorabji and stressed the importance of creating opportunities for women lawyers to assume greater responsibilities within the profession. Drawing upon his experience as a practising lawyer, the Chief Justice said the legal fraternity must remain responsive to changing societal expectations and technological advancements. He cautioned that institutions failing to adapt to emerging technologies risked being left behind. Describing lawyers as important custodians of constitutional rights and access to justice, Justice Bhati emphasised the need for cooperation between the Bench and the Bar to strengthen the justice delivery system. Earlier, interacting with judicial officers at the District Court Complex, the Chief Justice urged them to discharge their responsibilities fearlessly, compassionately and with an unwavering commitment to the rule of law. He said the judiciary had a crucial responsibility to safeguard citizens' rights, ensure access to justice and maintain public confidence in judicial institutions. Justice Bhati stressed that collective responsibility, mutual trust and institutional harmony were essential for the effective functioning of courts. He encouraged judicial officers to work collaboratively, maintain the highest standards of judicial conduct and create a peaceful and conducive working environment. Expressing satisfaction with the professional competence and dedication of judicial officers serving in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, the Chief Justice also highlighted the importance of continuous learning and guidance from senior judicial officers. Principal District and Sessions Judge Srinagar Naseer Ahmad Dar welcomed the Chief Justice and reaffirmed the district judiciary's commitment to quality adjudication, timely disposal of cases and reduction of pendency. At the felicitation programme, Kashmir Advocates Association president Waseem Gul highlighted the role of district courts as the first accessible forum of justice for ordinary citizens. He emphasised the importance of constructive cooperation between the Bench and the Bar and sought the Chief Justice's guidance on improving court infrastructure and facilities for lawyers and litigants. Gul also called for strengthening legal aid services, promoting alternative dispute resolution mechanisms and introducing structured training programmes for young advocates. He assured the Association's cooperation in improving the administration of justice and welcomed the newly appointed Principal District and Sessions Judge Srinagar. The Chief Justice appreciated the Association's decision to include women lawyers in its executive body and reiterated the need for professional cooperation, technological adaptation and inclusive participation in the legal system. The interactions focused on strengthening judicial institutions, improving access to justice and preserving the dignity and independence of the judiciary.

The Supreme Court on Monday took suo motu cognizance of recent cases of rape in Delhi-NCR, including a gangrape in a park and the alleged sexual assault of a minor inside a moving sleeper bus in Delhi.

A bench comprising Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran observed that they were distressed by the news reports regarding recurring sexual offences in the National Capital Region, and stressed the need to fix accountability.
In the order, the bench referred to the gangrape and murder of a teenage girl in Swarup Nagar in Delhi, where the police recovered the victim's decomposed body in a field.

Referring to the sexual assault of a minor in a moving sleeping bus, which the police failed to intercept during its travel of 47 kilometres from Greater Noida to Delhi, the Court said that “one cannot help but draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012.”
The Supreme Court on Monday (September 28) issued a set of immediate directions to the Delhi.
Police and civic authorities to secure public spaces in Delhi-NCR.
The directions include a survey of vulnerable areas, a district-wise vulnerability map, patrolling at all identified parks, and a lighting and CCTV audit.
All are to be completed within four weeks.

article_sentences: Guwahati: Supreme Court judge Justice Vikram Nath has underscored the pivotal role of legal education in fostering a just, equitable, and inclusive society.

Attending the fourth convocation ceremony of the National Law University and Judicial Academy, Assam (NLUJAA) at Srimanta Sankaradeva Kalakshetra here on Saturday as chief guest, Nath exhorted the graduating students to uphold the highest standards of professional ethics, constitutional values, and integrity while navigating the multifaceted challenges of the legal profession.
Presided over by Gauhati High Court Chief Justice and NLUJAA Chancellor Justice Ashutosh Kumar, the convocation was also attended by Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan as guest of honour.
Addressing the graduating students, Bhuyan emphasised that "human dignity" and "self-respect" constitute the highest and indispensable dimensions of human rights.
In his address, Kumar extended his heartfelt congratulations to the graduating students and inspired them to emerge as steadfast custodians of justice, integrity and public service.

He further emphasised the importance of discharging their professional responsibilities with an unwavering commitment to the larger interests of society and the enduring principles of constitutional morality.

On the occassion, NLUJAA Vice-Chancellor Prof (Dr) KVS Sharma presented the university's annual report, outlining its academic achievements, research initiatives, institutional endeavours and strategic vision for the future.

stories.title: Ranji Trophy 2026-27: Defending champion J&K begins title defence against Madhya Pradesh
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir’s strengths and vulnerabilities were on display in its Irani Cup 2026 defeat, but it will be bolstered by the return of Auqib Nabi fresh off his debut for the national team.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A week after the Irani Cup defeat exposed the cracks in its armour, Jammu and Kashmir gets a chance to reset on familiar turf.
The defending champion begins its Ranji Trophy campaign against Madhya Pradesh at the Sher-i-Kashmir Stadium on Sunday, hoping to leave that disappointment behind and find its feet again.
India pacer Auqib Nabi’s availability offers a timely boost, although J&K has rested Umar Nazir, who claimed six wickets in the Irani Cup.
Nasir Lone and Sunil Kumar provide further pace options, while Umran Malik, despite being with the squad, has not been considered.
The bigger concern, however, is the batting.
J&K squandered a first-innings lead against Rest of India before collapsing in the second innings.
Shubham Khajuria, Qamran Iqbal, Abdul Samad and captain Paras Dogra will need to shoulder the responsibility if the host is to make its home advantage count.
Building partnerships and avoiding another collapse will be central to its plans.
Madhya Pradesh, meanwhile, has spent the past week in Srinagar acclimatising to the conditions and arrives without any injury concerns.
Led by Shubham Sharma, it will miss Rajat Patidar and Venkatesh Iyer but retains considerable batting depth through Yash Dubey, Harsh Gawli and Himanshu Mantri.
The bowling attack, spearheaded by the experienced Avesh Khan and featuring Kuldeep Sen, has the pace to trouble the hosts.
Saransh Jain and Kumar Kartikeya add experience to the spin department, giving MP a balanced attack.

stories.headline: Concrete swallows Kashmir’s floodplains as natural defences shrink
stories.title: Concrete swallows Kashmir’s floodplains as natural defences shrink
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 10: Kashmir’s natural flood defences are steadily coming under pressure as concrete spreads across the Jhelum floodplain, wetlands lose ground and settlements expand into landscapes that once helped absorb excess water. A scientific study of the Jhelum basin has quantified the scale of this transformation: built-up land within the river’s floodplain increased from 55.47 square kilometres in 1972 to 203.30 square kilometres in 2013 — nearly fourfold in 41 years. “The population living within the floodplain also rose from 11.29 lakh in 1981 to 30.21 lakh in 2011, while the length of metalled roads increased from approximately 745.64 kilometres in 1962 to 1,698.23 kilometres in 2016,” the study notes. The findings, published in a study examining the climatic, geomorphic and human-induced drivers of the devastating September 2014 floods, reveal how rapidly development has transformed the Valley’s flood-prone landscape. The expansion matters because floodplains are not simply vacant stretches of land beside rivers. They form part of a natural system that accommodates excess water, while wetlands and drainage channels help regulate its movement. Construction, paved surfaces and obstructions can reduce water absorption, increase runoff and expose more people and infrastructure to inundation. The study also found that the area of major wetlands larger than 25 hectares in the Jhelum basin declined from 288.96 square kilometres in 1972 to 266.45 square kilometres in 2013, a reduction of 22.51 square kilometres. Researchers reported that 20 wetlands in and around Srinagar had been converted into urban colonies over five decades. Speaking to Rising Kashmir, senior environmentalist and researcher Dr Tanvir Ahmad Khan said: “Kashmir is committing an ecological blunder by allowing concrete to swallow its floodplains, wetlands and natural drainage systems. These are not wastelands available for urban expansion; they are nature’s own defence mechanisms against flooding. Every encroached floodplain and every reclaimed wetland weakens the Valley’s ability to absorb excess water and increases the vulnerability of people and property.” He said that the devastating floods of 2014 should have served as a permanent warning. “Yet, unplanned construction, indiscriminate land-use changes and the shrinking of natural water-retention areas continue to undermine Kashmir’s ecological security. The most disturbing aspect is that development often proceeds at the cost of the very natural systems that protect human settlements,” Khan said. “The government cannot claim environmental responsibility while allowing ecological buffers to disappear. Flood management must begin with protecting floodplains, restoring wetlands, removing illegal encroachments through lawful processes, and enforcing scientifically informed land-use regulations.” Khan said concrete may generate immediate economic gains, but when it replaces nature’s defences, society ultimately pays the price. “Kashmir cannot afford another warning written in floodwater,” he said. “The tragedy is that we are destroying nature’s protective infrastructure and expecting engineering and environmental mitigation measures and interventions to compensate for its loss. Embankments and drainage channels cannot fully replace functioning floodplains and wetlands.” The environmentalist said that the most alarming concern is the lack of political will to protect Kashmir’s floodplains, with short-term development interests repeatedly taking precedence over long-term ecological security and public safety. Dr Touseef Ahmad Bhat, a Kashmir-based environmentalist and socio-environmental activist, has repeatedly highlighted the interconnected nature of the Valley’s ecosystems. “Entire Kashmir is a wetland,” Bhat said, stressing the ecological importance of the region’s natural water systems. He also identified urbanisation, pollution, encroachment, land-use change and climate change among the pressures affecting wetlands, warning of consequences for biodiversity, water quality and human health. The concern is supported by research linking urban expansion and wetland loss with greater flood vulnerability. A 2023 study examining surface runoff in the Kashmir Valley found that rainfall exceeding 500 millimetres in the catchments played a key role in flooding, with northern catchments generating approximately 59.6 per cent of total runoff. It also identified built-up areas near rivers and below 1,560 metres as being at high risk of inundation. The evidence underlines the need to examine climate and land-use changes together. Heavy rainfall can trigger flooding, but the condition of floodplains, river channels and drainage networks influences how water moves through settlements. opening: Srinagar, Oct 10: Kashmir’s natural flood defences are steadily coming under pressure as concrete spreads across the Jhelum floodplain, wetlands lose ground and settlements expand into landscapes that once helped absorb excess water.

A scientific study of the Jhelum basin has quantified the scale of this transformation: built-up land within the river’s floodplain increased from 55.47 square kilometres in 1972 to 203.30 square kilometres in 2013 — nearly fourfold in 41 years.
body: “The population living within the floodplain also rose from 11.29 lakh in 1981 to 30.21 lakh in 2011, while the length of metalled roads increased from approximately 745.64 kilometres in 1962 to 1,698.23 kilometres in 2016,” the study notes.

The findings, published in a study examining the climatic, geomorphic and human-induced drivers of the devastating September 2014 floods, reveal how rapidly development has transformed the Valley’s flood-prone landscape.
The expansion matters because floodplains are not simply vacant stretches of land beside rivers.
They form part of a natural system that accommodates excess water, while wetlands and drainage channels help regulate its movement.
Construction, paved surfaces and obstructions can reduce water absorption, increase runoff and expose more people and infrastructure to inundation.

The study also found that the area of major wetlands larger than 25 hectares in the Jhelum basin declined from 288.96 square kilometres in 1972 to 266.45 square kilometres in 2013, a reduction of 22.51 square kilometres.
Researchers reported that 20 wetlands in and around Srinagar had been converted into urban colonies over five decades.

Speaking to Rising Kashmir, senior environmentalist and researcher Dr Tanvir Ahmad Khan said: “Kashmir is committing an ecological blunder by allowing concrete to swallow its floodplains, wetlands and natural drainage systems.
These are not wastelands available for urban expansion; they are nature’s own defence mechanisms against flooding.

Every encroached floodplain and every reclaimed wetland weakens the Valley’s ability to absorb excess water and increases the vulnerability of people and property.” He said that the devastating floods of 2014 should have served as a permanent warning.
“Yet, unplanned construction, indiscriminate land-use changes and the shrinking of natural water-retention areas continue to undermine Kashmir’s ecological security.
The most disturbing aspect is that development often proceeds at the cost of the very natural systems that protect human settlements,” Khan said.
“The government cannot claim environmental responsibility while allowing ecological buffers to disappear.

Flood management must begin with protecting floodplains, restoring wetlands, removing illegal encroachments through lawful processes, and enforcing scientifically informed land-use regulations.” Khan said concrete may generate immediate economic gains, but when it replaces nature’s defences, society ultimately pays the price.
“Kashmir cannot afford another warning written in floodwater,” he said.
“The tragedy is that we are destroying nature’s protective infrastructure and expecting engineering and environmental mitigation measures and interventions to compensate for its loss.

Embankments and drainage channels cannot fully replace functioning floodplains and wetlands.” The environmentalist said that the most alarming concern is the lack of political will to protect Kashmir’s floodplains, with short-term development interests repeatedly taking precedence over long-term ecological security and public safety.
Dr Touseef Ahmad Bhat, a Kashmir-based environmentalist and socio-environmental activist, has repeatedly highlighted the interconnected nature of the Valley’s ecosystems.
“Entire Kashmir is a wetland,” Bhat said, stressing the ecological importance of the region’s natural water systems.

He also identified urbanisation, pollution, encroachment, land-use change and climate change among the pressures affecting wetlands, warning of consequences for biodiversity, water quality and human health.
The concern is supported by research linking urban expansion and wetland loss with greater flood vulnerability.

A 2023 study examining surface runoff in the Kashmir Valley found that rainfall exceeding 500 millimetres in the catchments played a key role in flooding, with northern catchments generating approximately 59.6 per cent of total runoff.
It also identified built-up areas near rivers and below 1,560 metres as being at high risk of inundation.
The evidence underlines the need to examine climate and land-use changes together.
Heavy rainfall can trigger flooding, but the condition of floodplains, river channels and drainage networks influences how water moves through settlements.
The Jhelum’s flood-management system also depends on the Flood Spill Channel, which diverts excess water from the main river.
Designed to carry 8,000 cusecs, the channel requires adequate maintenance and protection against obstructions to preserve its intended function.
Satellite imagery of 63 sampled lakes showed that seven were no longer visible or had almost dried up.
The audit also found that 2,528.10 kanals of Hokersar Lake had been encroached upon amid the absence of proper survey and demarcation.

stories.headline: Protests in Delhi: SC directs no illegal detention, restoration of internet and metro services
stories.title: Protests in Delhi: SC directs no illegal detention, restoration of internet and metro services
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 11: The Supreme Court on Sunday directed that people gathering peacefully should not be illegally detained, as it issued a notice to the Centre on a plea seeking contempt proceedings for alleged violation of the court's direction to ensure that there is no "complete prohibition" on metro and train services in Delhi due to the CJP protest. In a special sitting, a bench of justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to ensure that Delhi Metro functions as per its normal schedule, and that there is no disruption to internet services, subject to law and order conditions. "In view of the urgent applications alleging violation of our earlier order dt. October 9, 2026, and also alleging illegal detention of large number of individuals at Delhi on October 10, 2026 this court had assembled for an urgent hearing. "Senior counsels submitted there was a flagrant violation of the directions -- metro railway was not functioning, New Delhi and Nizamuddin railway stations remained closed, no traffic advisories were issued and a large number of persons were subjected to undue harassment and illegal detention even beyond the area which was covered by the prohibitory order under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023," the bench said. The apex court also asked Mehta to ensure that lawyers, journalists and others shall not be impeded in discharging their professional duties. During the hearing, Mehta submitted that entry and exit were restricted at only 45 out of 303 stations across the metro network on October 10. As the hearing commenced, the top court said it would grant hearing to all lawyers while dealing with a plea seeking contempt proceedings against authorities for alleged blatant violation of the court's direction on the matter. The top court was also hearing a habeas petition filed by senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy against the detention of political leaders. The contempt plea, filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, has arrayed Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation chairperson D Thara as respondents. The petition referred to the top court's October 9 order, which was passed while hearing a separate plea against the closure of 57 metro stations and cancellation of trains to Delhi in view of the protest. The protest call was given by the CJP and some student organisations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission. The government thwarted a planned mass mobilisation at Jantar Mantar on Saturday after an unprecedented security clampdown and the detention of over 7,000 protesters, including CJP leader Abhijit Dipke, several opposition leaders and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.
